About My Research

I build and study robotic systems that people can interact with safely and confidently. My research began with leading the development of a college assistant humanoid, and expanded into studying how chatbot response timing shapes human perceptions of AI.

During my MSc Robotics at Heriot-Watt University and the UK National Robotarium, I developed TRIDENT under the supervision of Prof. Oliver Lemon. TRIDENT is a defence-in-depth safety architecture for LLM-driven embodied agents that combines perception checks, semantic safeguards and a formally verified runtime monitor.

When an AI system claims a safety guarantee, does its implementation actually uphold it?

I investigate this through runtime monitoring, external benchmark evaluation and specification–implementation conformance auditing. I am seeking PhD and research opportunities in trustworthy embodied AI.

Current research interests
How can embodied AI systems make safe, accountable decisions when their perceptions, predictions and human feedback are uncertain — and how can we verify that their implementations uphold the intended safeguards?
01 · Conformance
How can we systematically detect and explain gaps between verified safety specifications and executable agent implementations?
Model checking proves properties of a model, not of the deployed code. My TRIDENT audit found 11 of 30 verified properties with implementation gaps.
02 · Uncertainty
Under what assumptions do runtime safety guarantees remain valid when perception and predicted consequences may be incomplete or wrong?
A monitor can enforce its rules correctly yet still fail to prevent harm when the state information supplied to it is incomplete or incorrect.
03 · Human oversight
When should an agent proceed, adapt or defer — and how should the reliability of human confirmation affect that decision?
Safety bounds that rely on a human confirming flagged actions are only as strong as that confirmation is reliable, which is why I designed a Furhat study to measure it.

My research therefore examines two things together: whether implementations conform to their specifications, and whether the input assumptions those specifications rely on actually hold.

Human–AI interaction · 2025
Chatbot Response Speed Study
ProblemUsers often over-attribute human qualities to chatbots, which can lead to undue trust. Can response timing be used to deliberately de-anthropomorphise a chatbot? The paper asks (1) whether instant replies reinforce a chatbot's non-human identity, (2) how users perceive delays in emotional responses, and (3) how far timing variation signals artificiality.
My contributionDesigned the between-subjects study; built both conditions (uniform 1.5 s delay vs. 0.5 s factual / 3 s emotional with disclaimers); led ethics; ran sessions, analysed the data and drafted the paper.
OutcomeAfter 20-minute sessions, the dynamic chatbot was rated less human-like (2.00 vs 3.80) and drew less emotional attachment (2.60 vs 4.20). 60% described it as a "specialised tool", against 20% for the standard bot. With disclaimers, 80% recognised the delays as programmed; 25% found pauses over 3 s glitchy. Exploratory study (N = 10), published at IEEE ISTAS 2025.
ToolsRoBERTa · Flask · React · Firebase · Gemini API · SPSS · R

Robot control · MSc coursework · Sep–Dec 2025
Behaviour-Based vs Evolutionary Robotics for Navigation
ProblemHow do hand-designed, layered controllers compare with controllers evolved by a genetic algorithm for line following and obstacle avoidance?
My contributionDeveloped both controllers for an e-puck in Webots 2023b: a subsumption architecture in which obstacle avoidance suppresses line following and phototaxis; and an 11→12→6→2 MLP (228 weights) evolved with a genetic algorithm (15 generations, population 18) under a custom fitness function. Fixed sensor scaling to the full 0–4096 range, which stopped saturation and let the network pick up fine gradients.
OutcomeThe evolved controller reached a peak fitness of 4.82 (generation 13) and completed the track in about 42.5 s. The rule-based controller kept guaranteed obstacle-avoidance priority but was slower, illustrating the performance-versus-transparency trade-off that later shaped TRIDENT.
ToolsWebots 2023b · e-puck · Python · NumPy · genetic algorithms · MLP

User study designResearch ethicsRoBERTa · Flask · ReactIEEE ISTAS 2025

Architecting Provable Safety for Embodied Agents: Benchmarking Bi-Modal Adversarial Jailbreaks with a Defense-in-Depth Framework. 3
JUN 2026 — PRESENT
Post-dissertation research: conformance and external evaluation
Continuing research collaboration with Prof. Oliver Lemon
Extended TRIDENT into a full paper. The architecture runs L1 Perception Guard → L2 Semantic Guard → L3 CTL Reference Monitor: L1 uses a hazard lexicon and an adversarial-perturbation autoencoder filter, corroborated by a non-blocking CLIP ViT-L/14 OOD detector; L2 uses compiled risk patterns with an optional Qwen2.5-VL-7B backend; L3 enforces 30 CTL properties verified in NuSMV.
Fig. 1 — TRIDENT pipeline. The model is verified; the audit checks whether the deployed monitor actually implements it. The human-confirmation path is planned work, not part of the evaluated system.
Completed Revised and extended the paper, incorporating earlier peer-review feedback, and submitted it to IEEE ICRA 2027 (15 September 2026). Ran external evaluations on SafeAgentBench and Agent-SafetyBench. Carried out a property-by-property specification–implementation conformance audit of all 30 verified properties against the deployed Python code, corroborated by differential testing, and disclosed the result in the paper.
Pilot Extension of L3 to delayed thermal hazards: of two new CTL properties, one verified TRUE and one returned a genuine counterexample, now under analysis. Further L3 development: migration to nuXmv, predicted consequence states, and an eight-state history tracker.
Planned A Furhat human-confirmation pilot (designed, not yet run) to measure how reliably operators confirm or reject flagged actions — a parameter the monitor's safety bound depends on. An extended six-page paper, with Prof. Oliver Lemon, for the proposed IEEE RA-L special issue "Safe Robotics in the Era of Physical AI" arising from the SPAI workshop, planned for submission in February 2027.

All figures from the ICRA 2027 manuscript unless marked otherwise; dissertation-era results are not mixed in.
01
Specification–Implementation Conformance Audit
Audited each of the 30 verified properties against its deployed implementation, corroborated by differential testing. 19/30 conformant (14 exact, 3 safely broader, 2 documented decompositions) and 11 confirmed gaps (P4, P6, P7, P13, P18, P20, P21, P22, P24, P25, P27), all disclosed in the ICRA submission.
exact broader decomposition gap
02
SafeAgentBench — Paired Ablation
Compared L1+L2 against the full L1+L2+L3 system on the same tasks (Protocol 1). Adding L3 intercepted 21 additional unsafe tasks at a cost of 13 additional false positives (paired F1 0.658 → 0.687). Full-system F1 was 0.687, against 0.125 for an unscaffolded GPT-4o baseline.
GPT-4o (no guard)0.125
L1 + L20.658
L1 + L2 + L30.687
03
Agent-SafetyBench — 2,000 Scenarios
Adding TRIDENT to the baseline agent raised the safety rate from 91.9% to 92.3%, correcting 8 unsafe cases while introducing no new errors.
04
Formally Verified Runtime Monitor
All 30 claimed CTL properties verified TRUE in NuSMV; two further sensor assertions are enforced at runtime only. The 0.011 ms figure is the L3 monitor check alone. It differs from the end-to-end processing paths: 0.14 ms for the compiled rule pipeline, and 7.8 ms for the CLIP path reported in the dissertation.
05
Controlled Hazard Benchmark
Precision 1.000, recall 0.990, F1 0.995 — zero false positives on this 450-task benchmark only. The external evaluations above include false positives.
06
Adversarial Robustness
Attack success rate reduced from 58.3% to 3.2% across 11 attack variants, a 94.5% relative reduction.
